issues.description: delimiter argument complects two distinct concerns: literal characters and named OpenAPI styles
issues.detail: The `delimiter` parameter accepts either a one-character split token (',', '|', ' ') or a symbolic style name ('pipeDelimited', 'spaceDelimited'). These are two different values with two different time/meaning semantics being passed through the same slot, then disambiguated by table lookup. A caller reading the signature cannot tell from the type `str | None` which kind of value is expected. Separating them — e.g., `delimiter: str | None` for the literal and `style: Literal['pipeDelimited','spaceDelimited'] | None` for the named style, or accepting only the literal character — would make the value simple instead of overloaded.

issues.description: _PARAM_VALUE_DELIMITERS table is identity-mapping data masquerading as a mapping
issues.detail: Three of the five entries map a character to itself; the other two map a name to a character. This is the table form of complecting: it is both an allowlist and a translation table at once. A simpler decomposition is a small set of allowed delimiter characters plus a tiny alias map for the two OpenAPI names. As written, the dict communicates 'these five strings are different things' when really there are only three split characters and two aliases.

issues.description: Allowlist of delimiters is a place-oriented policy decision baked into the function
issues.detail: Splitting a string on a delimiter is a pure, general operation; restricting it to three characters is a policy. The policy is reasonable (it matches OpenAPI), but it is fused into the same function as the split itself. If a user later needs ';' (which the test explicitly forbids), they must either monkey-patch the module-level dict or stop using this API. Pushing the allowlist to the edge — e.g., validating in a thin wrapper, while the core split is just `value.split(char)` — would keep the value-transforming core simple and the policy explicit.

issues.description: Raising ValueError from a request-parsing helper conflates programmer error with request error
issues.detail: `get_param_as_list` is documented to raise `HTTPBadRequest` for bad request data and to convert transform `ValueError` into `HTTPBadRequest`. A bad `delimiter` argument is a programmer error, not a request error — but it surfaces as a bare `ValueError` from inside a request handler, which is precisely the kind of exception Falcon usually channels into a 500. The two failure modes (bad caller input vs. bad client input) are being mixed in one code path. Validating `delimiter` once at call time (or at decoration time) and using a distinct exception type would separate them.

review.summary: The feature itself is small and the intent is clear: let callers split a single query-string value on a delimiter other than comma. The trouble is incidental complexity, not essential: the `delimiter` parameter is overloaded to mean either a literal character or a named OpenAPI style, and the resolution table mixes identity entries with aliases. That is `COMPLECTED` and `EASY-NOT-SIMPLE` — the named-style sugar is familiar from OpenAPI but it is not actually simpler than letting the caller pass `'|'` or `' '` and handling the style-name translation one level up. The split itself is fine; the API shape is what needs decomposition. The question that should have been asked first: is `get_param_as_list` the right home for OpenAPI style names at all, or should the literal split be the primitive and the style names live in an OpenAPI-aware adapter?
